idiom_name: struct { double amount; unit_t unit } plus one conversion table (C11)
implementation_notes: C has no units, no operator overloading and no generic numeric types, so the classic Quantity class degrades to a plain struct that pairs the amount with a unit code, plus functions that operate on it: constructors such as metres(), a single static conversion table keyed by the unit code, and accessors such as quantity_in(). Put the unit inside the struct (cppreference, struct declaration) rather than in the variable name, because that is the only place it can live: C11 generic selection dispatches on C types, and feet, metres and seconds are all double, so it cannot make unit mixing a compile error. The classic object-oriented form - a vtable of unit objects with conversion ratios - is justified only when units are added at run time from configuration or a database.
pitfalls: The conversion table holds double factors, so most imperial conversions are approximations; use scaled integers or document the precision when a value must round-trip.
Passing raw doubles around next to the struct defeats the pattern: the compiler cannot tell a length in feet from one in metres, so the raw amount must be unreachable outside the accessor functions.
A switch on the unit enum without a default case lets a newly added unit fall through to an identity or wrong conversion instead of failing.
